body.text: In short:
Half of young Australian adults aged 18 to 29 are now living at home with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001.
Australians are more stressed about housing and money, and half of workers feel they are over-educated for their job, but their long-term relationships are relatively strong.
What's next?
The latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey has shown how peoples' lives have changed between 2001 and 2024.
Australia, we have good news, bad news and confirmation about life's hardships that is no news to anyone.

The bad news, according to a quarter century of data on social and economic trends that shape the nation, is that we're more stressed about housing and money, tired, worried about our cognitive health, living much longer at home as young adults, and half of us have jobs we're over-qualified for.
The good news is employment is high, many more women hold university degrees, and our long-term relationships are in pretty good health.

That's the snapshot of the nation from this year's Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) annual survey, which "shows both the joys and the challenges of life", says lead author Dr Inga Lass.

Drawing on data collected from 2001 to 2024, the annual HILDA report is the largest longitudinal study of its kind in Australia, following the same 17,000 people each year for insights into how our lives are changing.
It tracks issues including housing affordability and housing stress, labour market mismatches, relationship quality, cognitive health, and financial stress, among many other things.
Noticeable rise in young adults living at home for longer
This year's survey found half of young adults aged 18 to 29 were living with their parents in 2024, up from 39 per cent in 2001.

Two-thirds of young adults who had left the parental home were renting privately, but young renters also reported higher rates of housing inadequacy and lower satisfaction than those who remained with parents or who entered home ownership.

Housing stress among young mortgage holders has remained relatively stable over the last two decades, ranging from 8.6 per cent in 2001 to 9.9 per cent in 2024, despite substantial increases in housing costs.
The report's authors say that suggests that mortgage entry has become increasingly restricted to young adults with higher earnings, substantial savings or access to family wealth.
"For the majority of young adults who rent privately, the picture is more concerning," it says.
"In mainland capital cities, 25.3 per cent of young private renters are now in housing stress, up from 17.6 per cent for the equivalent cohort in 2001," it says.
Workers are better educated, but half feel over-qualified for their jobs
The report says half of Australian workers feel over-qualified for their job, and a quarter feel over-skilled.

Both types of mismatches are more prevalent among younger workers below 25 years of age, in certain occupations (e.g. sales workers, labourers), and in certain industries (e.g. accommodation and food services).
"With 50 per cent of Australian workers reporting they believe they are over-educated for their role, we're exactly where we were in 2012,"

"This suggests that the labour market has broadly kept up with increasing educational levels, with the number of jobs that require bachelor's or master's degrees growing the fastest, and jobs that require a maximum of Year 11 of schooling or less education declining."
Being born in a non-English speaking country and having a casual work contract are associated with higher probabilities of both over-education and over-skilling.
Job mismatches are associated with lower job and life satisfaction, and a higher probability of job quitting, with over-skilling generally having stronger negative effects than over-education.

The trend growth in the educational attainment of women has continued throughout the last quarter-century: well over half of women aged 25 to 44 now hold a university degree (compared to 40 per cent of men in that age group).
Men's educational attainment has also grown, but much more slowly. As a result, in all age groups below 65, women now have considerably higher educational attainment than men.
The report highlights that a particular demographic is being left behind:

"Men aged 25 to 44 who did not complete Year 12 have become less likely to be in full-time work and more likely to be outside the labour force," report co-author Dr Kyle Peyton said. "Their full-time employment rate fell from 70 per cent in 2001 to 63 per cent in 2024, while the share outside the labour force rose from 12 per cent to 22 per cent."
"Men aged 25 to 44 who did not complete Year 12 have become less likely to be in full-time work and more likely to be outside the labour force," report co-author Dr Kyle Peyton said.
"Their full-time employment rate fell from 70 per cent in 2001 to 63 per cent in 2024, while the share outside the labour force rose from 12 per cent to 22 per cent."
Life partnerships are very strong

But the survey also found that most Australians in long-term relationships (married or otherwise) feel their relationship is very strong, although men consistently report higher relationship satisfaction than women.
When asked to answer questions about the quality of one's relationship across six dimensions, on a scale of 1 to 5, high scores dominated across all six dimensions.

Questions about love received the highest ratings overall, but questions about how well one's partner meets one's needs and to what extent the relationship meets one's original expectations scored the lowest ratings.
An equal division of housework, child care and earnings were significant predictors of stronger relationship quality.
Couples caring for children, living with disability, or experiencing financial stress tended to report lower relationship scores.

Relationship quality is highest among childless couples with relatively even earnings (who also tend to share paid and unpaid work relatively equally) and lowest in couples with dependent children where the woman is the primary earner (and who typically undertakes most paid and unpaid work).

Relationship quality is also highest among recent unions and very long-term unions, but notably lower for relationships of intermediate duration, reaching its lowest point about 24 years after partners move in together.

"When you think about the trajectory of a relationship, there's a good chance that potentially stressful factors like work, bills and raising children start to ease around the 25-year mark, allowing couples to prioritise their relationship," Dr Lass said.
Employment high, but more people suffering financial and housing stress
The survey notes that most of the interviews in the survey were conducted between July and October 2024.
Around that time, the consumer price index (CPI) increased by roughly 19.5 per cent between the December quarter of 2019 and the September quarter of 2024.
Over that same period, the rent price index increased by around 16.8 per cent, and the Reserve Bank had hiked interest rates rapidly a couple of years earlier.
The survey found that stagnant wages and the increased cost of living had cancelled out any feelings about the vast improvement in employment in 2024.
"Employment rates have jumped dramatically, particularly for women, since the survey started in 2001," report co-author Professor Roger Wilkins said.

"However, our earnings are not rising enough to keep up with the big increases in housing costs and other non-discretionary spending, so the average person is likely to be under more financial pressure."
The survey found that the hourly gender wage gap reached 10.2 per cent in 2024, which was the second-lowest since 2001.
But some large gender disparities remain, with 43 per cent of women working full-time, compared to 70 per cent of men.
